title: Square up a racked face frame by its diagonal
instruction: The glued-up face frame on the bench is racked out of square. Make it square, so that its two corner-to-corner diagonals are equal, keep it on its outline, then let go of it.
context: Cabinetmakers and bench carpenters (O*NET 51-7011.00, 47-2031.00) check a glued-up frame by measuring its two diagonals and squeeze the long one, pushing its two corners toward each other, before the glue sets. It differs from squaring a rigid beam between guide rails or pushing a part in evenly: here the part itself changes shape under two opposed forces on different members, and a single push only slides it.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases, on the table (x forward, y left). Pine face frame, 0.30 kg, outer 16 deep x 30 wide: two 3 x 3 cm rails 30 cm long running left to right, near rail centred x 20.0 and far rail centred x 33.0, and two 3 cm wide, 1 cm high stiles between them at y +-13.5, with darker 3 cm corner blocks at the four rail ends. Each of the four joints is a stub tenon on the stile end, 10 mm wide (along the rail), 6 mm thick and 12 mm long, in a mortise 11.6 mm wide, 6.4 mm high and 13 mm deep, cut off-centre: with the frame square the tenon lies against one cheek of the mortise (0.05 mm fit) and the whole 1.6 mm of clearance is on the other side, so each stile can turn up to 6.6 degrees one way (far rail 15 mm to the left) and is stopped by the cheek about 0.5 mm of far-rail travel past square the other way. The stile's shoulders are cut back 2 mm on the opening side so they do not bind. The start (8 mm, 3.5 degrees) is inside that range. The tenons carry a film of PVA wood glue that is still wet, so the far rail moves along its length under about 2 N. The far rail starts 8 mm to the left of the near rail (y +0.8), so the diagonal from near-right to far-left is 14 mm longer than the other. Friction on the table 0.3. A yellow tape rectangle (0.4 cm wide) is stuck on the table 2 cm outside the outline of the squared frame, centred x 26.5, y 0.
scoring: Measured with a tape and a ruler. diff = difference between the two diagonals (corner block centres) at the end. 0 at once and for good if a corner is ever lifted more than 1 cm, any outer corner leaves the tape rectangle, or the far rail is pushed 15 mm from square (joint broken open). Otherwise 0 if diff is over 8 mm, 0.25 for 5 to 8 mm, 0.5 for 2 to 5 mm, and 0.5 for 2 mm or less until both grippers are at least 3 cm from the frame and it has moved less than 1 mm for 1 s; then 1.0.
reset_notes: Pull the joints apart, wipe them and spread a fresh thin film of PVA wood glue (or, for repeated trials, the same amount of white lithium grease) on all four tenons; push the frame together. Check with a ruler that the far rail can be pushed 15 mm to the left of the near rail and no more than 0.5 mm to the right of square. Check the shear resistance with a spring scale hooked on the far rail's end while the near rail is held: it should start to slide at 1.5 to 2.5 N; thin or thicken the film until it does. Set the far rail 8 mm to the left of the near rail (ruler against the near rail's end), and set the frame inside the tape rectangle with its rails parallel to the tape.
fidelity: The glued frame is a four-bar linkage modelled as one slider: the far rail slides along y on the near rail, from 15 mm left (the joints' turning limit, 6.6 degrees) to 0.5 mm past square (where the tenons meet their mortise cheeks), with 2 N of Coulomb friction; the stiles are hinges turned to match. Tenons and mortises are not drawn. The stiles are 1 cm high so the open fingers clear them. Rigid parts, friction 0.3 on the table.
